chapters.title: Introduction: A Writing Book About Writing Books
1: Murder Your Darlings. Keep Your Eye on Those Fancy Phrases.
2: Find and Cut the Clutter. Search for Lazy Words, Even After Several Drafts.
3: Learn to Live Inside Words. Recognize Both Their Literal Meanings and Their Associations.
4: Shape a Sentence for the Desired Effect. To Achieve Clarity, Put the Main Clause First, with Subject and Verb Together.
5: Work from a Plan. Include a Lead or an Intro You Can Write Without Referring to Notes
6: Recognize two contradictory meanings of style. Be prepared to abandon the agreed-upon style of a group to express your individual style.
7: Vary sentence length to create a pleasing rhythm. Think of each period as a stop sign.
8: Use visual markings to spark your creative process. Also use them to signify your revisions.
9: Tune your voice for the digital age. Experiment with language and forms of delivery.
10: Turn the dials that adjust the way you sound as a writer. Read the work aloud to make sure it sounds like you—or a little better.
"11: Learn the steps of the writing process. Good writing is not magic, but it’s full of surprises."
12: Keep writing; things will get better. Never be discouraged by the inadequacies of early drafts.
13: Write freely to discover what you want to say. Use a “zero draft” to move you toward a first draft.
"14: Say it loud: “I am a writer.” Assume the identity of a writer, especially at moments of self-doubt."
"15: Develop the writing habit. Find a reliable work space, free of distractions, where you can aim for a daily level of production."
16: Understand the value of storytelling. Guide readers in identifying dangers to avoid and people who will help.
17: Prefer the complex human narrator. Try alternatives to the all-knowing or completely unreliable storyteller.
"18: Write for sequence, then for theme. Readers want to know what happens next and also what it all means."
19: Distill your story into five words—maybe three. Use the “premise” or other tools to articulate what your work is really about.
20: Add dimension to characters. Flat ones are useful; round ones feel more human.
21: Report for story. Gather what you need to make nonfiction read like a novel.
22: Anticipate the needs of readers. Deliver urgent information or compelling narratives.
23: Embrace rhetoric as the source of language power. Use it to move your best words out of hiding.
24: Influence the emotional responses of your audience. Drive readers and viewers to the conflicting emotions of pity and fear.
"25: Sign a social contract with the reader. Be transparent about your methods, especially with memoir and the personal essay."
"26: Write to the level of your reader—and a little higher. Learn the tricks that make a text easy to read or, if you prefer, hard."
27: Learn the strategies that make reports reliable. Monitor your bias and unload your language.
28: Write to make your soul grow. Transform the disadvantage of suffering into the redemptive advantage of powerful writing.
"29: Write to delight and instruct. Often you can accomplish one or the other, but you are at your best when you can do both."
"30: Become the eyes and ears of the audience. Write from different visual and aural perspectives, from a distance and up close."
"31: Choose advocacy over propaganda. Never appeal to readers’ base instincts, and challenge those who do."
32: Be a writer—and so much more. Use all your resources to see the whole sky.
